1331.title: The Tibetan traditions, closed
1331.hook: four schools, the stages, mind training, the bardo
1331.howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhist practice, a session traditionally begins by recalling bodhicitta, the wish to awaken for the sake of all beings, and ends by dedicating whatever merit came from it to all beings.

segments.voice: Last week ended in Mongolia, with old monks coming forward to teach again. Your line: it returned. Today a long stretch of the path closes.

A Tibetan practitioner finishes a session of practice. Maybe it was prostrations, maybe a mantra, maybe a quiet sit by a butter lamp. Before standing up, there's one more thing. The hands come together, and a few lines are said, offering whatever good came from this practice to every living being, everywhere, without leaving anyone out. Then they get up and put the kettle on. It takes less than a minute. And it's a good place to stand while looking back over this stretch of the path, because nearly everything in the Tibetan traditions leans toward that one gesture.
screen: `A SESSION ENDS.` → `HANDS TOGETHER.` → `OFFERED TO EVERY BEING.`

segments.voice: The schools. Nyingma, the ancient one, tracing back to Padmasambhava and his hidden treasures. Kagyu, the line of Tilopa, Naropa, Marpa and Milarepa, with its long retreats and its songs. Sakya, the school of the gray earth, teaching that the path and its fruit are joined. Gelug, the school of Tsongkhapa, with its great monasteries, its debates, its geshes, and now its geshemas. Beside them, Jonang, the Rime movement that gathered teachings from many lineages, and Bon, Tibet's other tradition, with its own teachers and not a Buddhist school. The stages: the lamrim, step by step, a precious human life, death, karma, refuge, all beings as our mothers, and finally calm and insight. Mind training: Atisha's teaching, set out by Chekawa in seven points, sending and taking on the breath, bad circumstances as the path, the five strengths, two witnesses. The bardo: death and the in-between, the clear light, the peaceful and wrathful visions recognized as the mind's own display, and a book read aloud beside the dying. Around all of it: butter lamps, mani stones, thangkas painted by rule, the Kalachakra's sand swept away, tulkus returning, and the mountains from Ladakh to Mongolia. Different schools, different emphases. But each, in its own words, sets this practice inside bodhicitta: the wish to wake up for the sake of all beings. That's why a session ends with the dedication. Whatever was done was never only for oneself.
screen: `FOUR SCHOOLS, AND THEIR NEIGHBORS.` · `THE STAGES OF THE PATH.` · `MIND TRAINING IN SEVEN POINTS.` · `THE BARDO AND THE CLEAR LIGHT.` · then, large: `FOR ALL BEINGS.`

segments.voice: Wish someone you love well, then someone you barely know, a face from the street or the store, then someone difficult, and let the circle widen past every border to every being that breathes. As the time closes, let whatever good came from this sit go out to all of them, the way the practitioner did before putting the kettle on. If you pray, you can use a dedication from your own tradition.
The Tibetan traditions. Four schools and their neighbors, the stages, mind training and the bardo, all held inside the wish to wake up for all beings. Today's word.
Your line: for all beings. Tomorrow the path turns to other schools, starting in China. One stretch closed; the road goes on.

1332.title: Tiantai
1332.hook: the Chinese school built on the Lotus, founded by Zhiyi
1332.howItsDone: Tiantai Buddhists in China, and the Tendai school that grew from it in Japan, study and recite the Lotus Sutra and join that study with meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday the Tibetan traditions closed: the schools, the stages, mind training, the bardo. Your line: for all beings. Today the road turns east again.

What would you name a school after? Its founder, maybe. Its big idea. Its favorite book. This one carries the name of a mountain. A monk named Zhiyi went up into the hills to teach, and the place stuck to everything he taught there. Students came. Lectures were written down. A whole way of reading the Buddha grew on that slope, and wherever it traveled afterward, it kept the mountain's name. This path met Zhiyi once before, sorting a drawer full of sutras. Today, the school itself, and the one book at its center: Tiantai.
screen: `A SCHOOL NAMED FOR A MOUNTAIN.` → `ZHIYI GOES UP TO TEACH.` → `THE NAME TRAVELS WITH IT.`

segments.voice: Tiantai opens a new stretch of the path: other schools and movements, starting in China. Tradition names earlier teachers in its line, but Zhiyi is the one who gave it its shape, and the school is also known by another name: the Lotus school. Why the Lotus? This path spent a long stretch inside that sutra: the burning house and the carts, the son who wanders off and comes home not knowing he's the heir, the herbs that drink the same rain and grow to different heights, the monk who bows to everyone and says, you will become a Buddha. Zhiyi lectured on it line by line, and on its title, word by word. For Tiantai, the Lotus is where the Buddha finally says the whole of it: all the different paths were one vehicle all along. So a school built on that reading doesn't need to throw other teachings away. The simpler sutras, the strict rules, the long meditations: Tiantai keeps them, and reads each one as a step toward the same summit. Nothing is wasted; everything has a place on the one road. And it's a way of practice, not only a library. Tiantai joined study and meditation, the book and the cushion, and taught that you need both, the way a bird needs two wings. Over the next days come two of its treasures, the three truths and Zhiyi's practice of stopping and seeing, and later in this stretch the school crosses the sea to Japan.

segments.voice: Let one picture from the Lotus Sutra come back: the father calling his children out of a burning house, the son working in his own father's yard without knowing it, the rain falling the same on every plant, the monk who bows. Don't pick the best one; take the one that arrives. Hold it the way you'd hold a photograph, and let the breath keep going underneath it.

1333.title: Three truths
1333.hook: Tiantai: emptiness, the provisional and the middle, all at once
1333.howItsDone: Tiantai and Tendai Buddhists study the three truths, emptiness, the provisional and the middle, and use them as a way of contemplating any object or moment in meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tiantai, the school on Zhiyi's mountain. Your line: the Lotus school. Today, one of its treasures.

Make a fist. Go on, either hand. There it is: a fist. Now open your fingers. Where did the fist go? It didn't fly off anywhere. There was never a fist apart from the hand curled up a certain way. And yet, a moment ago, it was a real fist; you could have knocked on a door with it. So which is true: there's no fist, or there's a fist? Tiantai's answer is yes. And then it adds a third thing. Tiantai calls them the three truths.
screen: `MAKE A FIST.` → `OPEN IT. WHERE DID IT GO?` → `NO FIST, OR A FIST?`

segments.voice: It starts with a verse by the Indian teacher Nagarjuna, read in Chinese, which says in substance: whatever arises from conditions, that is emptiness; it is a name given in dependence; and that is the middle way. Zhiyi read that one verse and heard three truths in it. Emptiness: the fist has no fist-ness of its own. It's made of a hand, a moment, a squeeze; take those away and nothing is left over. The provisional: and still, the fist works. It has a name, it can knock, it's a real fist in the world of fists, even though it depends on everything else. The middle: the two aren't taking turns. The fist isn't empty on Monday and real on Tuesday. It is empty and real in the same instant, and the middle is simply that togetherness. Then Zhiyi's turn. Some teachers treated these as levels: first you see things as real, then you climb to see them as empty, then, at the top, the middle. Tiantai calls that one way of teaching. Its own reading is that the three are perfectly joined, each truth containing the other two. Look all the way into emptiness and the provisional world is right there; look closely at the plain world and the middle is right there. The school says this isn't a puzzle to win. It's a way of seeing a doorway, a quarrel, a face, without falling into either ditch, it's all nothing or it's all solid, and walking the middle of the road.
screen: `NAGARJUNA'S VERSE, READ THREE WAYS.` · `EMPTY. PROVISIONAL. MIDDLE.` · `NOT LEVELS, BUT JOINED.` · `NEITHER DITCH.` · then, large: `THREE AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Pick something in front of you, a pen, a shoe, your own hand, and for a few breaths look at it as empty: made of parts and causes, nothing in it that stands alone. Then for a few breaths look at it as provisional: it has a name, it does its job, it's really here. Then let both be true together, without choosing or straining for a special feeling, and breathe.
Three truths. Tiantai's teaching that every thing is empty, provisionally real, and the middle, all in one moment, each holding the others. Today's word.

1334.title: Calming and seeing
1334.hook: Zhiyi's meditation manual of stopping and seeing
1334.howItsDone: Tiantai and Tendai practitioners train in calming and contemplation together, often beginning with Zhiyi's practical advice on posture, breath, food and sleep before turning to contemplation of the mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three truths: empty, provisional, and the middle. Your line: three at once. Today, how Tiantai trains the eye to see that.

Stop. Look. Listen. Three words painted on a sign at a railroad crossing, and kids learn them in that order. Not look, then stop. You can't really look while you're still running; the feet have to come to rest before the eyes can do their work. A monk on a Chinese mountain built a whole meditation teaching on a pair of words that work the same way. First you stop. Then you see. His teaching on it comes down in a long work and a short one, and students still sit with them. Today's word is that pair: zhiguan.
screen: `STOP. LOOK. LISTEN.` → `REST THE FEET, THEN THE EYES WORK.` → `TWO WORDS, ONE PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Zhi means stopping, or calming: the mind settling, the way a stirred-up glass of pond water goes still and the silt sinks. Guan means seeing, or contemplation: looking clearly at what's there once the water has cleared. Behind the Chinese pair stand two older Indian words for the same practices, shamatha and vipashyana. Zhiyi's great meditation work, recorded by his student, is called Mohe Zhiguan, the great calming and seeing. It is long and demanding. Tradition also gives him a short manual, often called the small calming and seeing, written for beginners, and it's surprisingly practical. Before any talk of truths, it talks about adjusting your eating and your sleep, how to sit down and how to get up again, how to breathe so the breath is neither rough nor held. Zhiyi doesn't treat the two as separate hobbies, calming some days and seeing on others. Stopping without seeing, the tradition warns, can turn dull and sleepy. Seeing without stopping turns scattered, a flashlight swinging around a dark room. Together they steady each other. And what does the seeing actually see? In Tiantai, it looks into a single moment of mind and finds the three truths there: empty, provisional, and the middle. So the stopping isn't the goal. It's the stillness that lets the seeing happen, the feet coming to rest at the crossing so the eyes can do their work.
screen: `ZHI STOPS. GUAN SEES.` · `A GREAT BOOK AND A SMALL ONE.` · `NEITHER DULL NOR SCATTERED.` · `THE SEEING FINDS THE THREE TRUTHS.` · then, large: `STOP AND SEE.`

segments.voice: Settle your body the way the small manual says, not slumped, not stiff, the breath smooth and unforced, and for the first stretch only stop, resting on the breath while the silt settles. When things feel a little clearer, start to look at what's here, a sound, an ache, a passing thought, plainly, without chasing it. If you get scattered, stop again; if you get sleepy, look again.
Zhiguan. Stopping and seeing: calming the mind and looking clearly, practiced together as Zhiyi taught them. Today's word.

1335.title: Huayan
1335.hook: the school of the Flower Garland Sutra
1335.howItsDone: Huayan Buddhists study the Flower Garland Sutra and the writings of masters such as Fazang, and contemplate the interconnection of all things it describes; the sutra is also studied in Korea and Japan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, zhiguan: Zhiyi's stopping and seeing. Your line: stop and see. Today, a second Chinese school.

Two schools, one story. Chinese Buddhists told it like this. Right after the Buddha woke up under the tree, before he walked anywhere or taught anyone a simple word, he poured out a teaching so vast that the people around him couldn't follow it. They sat there, the story says, as if they could neither hear nor speak. So he started again, simpler. Tiantai heard that story and said: you see, the Buddha had to come down to meet people. Another school heard the very same story and said: you see, the first thing out of his mouth was the whole truth. That second school is today's word. Huayan.
screen: `THE FIRST TEACHING, TOO VAST.` → `TIANTAI: HE CAME DOWN TO MEET US.` → `ANOTHER SCHOOL: THAT WAS THE WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Tiantai was named for a mountain. Huayan is named for a book: Huayan is the Chinese title of the Avatamsaka Sutra, the Flower Garland. This path spent time inside that sutra earlier this year: Indra's net, the pilgrim Sudhana, the tower where every room holds all the others. Today, the people who made a school of it. Huayan remembers a line of masters who handed the teaching on. The one this path has met before is Fazang, the monk who explained the sutra to an empress using a golden lion. Like Tiantai, Huayan sorted the Buddha's teachings into kinds. Both schools kept every sutra, and both put one at the summit: for Tiantai, the Lotus; for Huayan, the Flower Garland, which its teachers call the round, or complete, teaching. Each school has its reasons, and Chinese Buddhists could study both. And the book at Huayan's center isn't a list of rules or a set of arguments. It's a vision. Light pours from the Buddha, worlds open inside worlds, and everything turns out to be woven into everything else. Huayan's teachers set themselves a hard job: to put that vision into words a person could study and practice. Next come two of the ways they tried, interpenetration and a golden lion. But it starts with a garland: many flowers, strung on one thread, each still its own flower.

1336.title: Interpenetration
1336.hook: Huayan: each thing contains all things, without blocking each other
1336.howItsDone: Huayan Buddhists contemplate the interpenetration of principle and event, and of each event with every other, drawing on the Flower Garland Sutra and the commentaries of masters such as Fazang and Chengguan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Huayan, the school named for a sutra. Your line: the flower garland. Today, the idea at that school's heart.

A lamp is already burning in the corner of the room. Someone comes in and lights a second one on the other side. The room gets brighter. But notice what doesn't happen. The second light doesn't shove the first one out of the way. There's no line down the middle where one lamp's light stops and the other's starts. Both lights fill the whole room, all of it, at the same time, and each is still its own flame. A school of Buddhist teachers in China said the whole world is built a little like that room. Their word for it is interpenetration.
screen: `A SECOND LAMP IS LIT.` → `NEITHER LIGHT SHOVES THE OTHER.` → `BOTH FILL THE WHOLE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Huayan teaches that each thing contains all things, and is contained in all things, and that they don't get in each other's way. The school's word for that last part is wu'ai: without obstruction. Take it a step at a time. Huayan teachers spoke of the deep nature of things, which they called principle, and of particular things, which they called events. A cup is an event. Its emptiness, the way it depends on everything else, is principle. Between principle and event, they said, there is no obstruction: the cup's emptiness isn't hiding behind the cup. It's right there in it. Then the bold step. Between one event and another there's no obstruction either. Not just the cup and its nature, but the cup and the table, the cup and the potter, the cup and the person drinking. Each one holds the others, the way each lamp's light holds the room and the other light too. That is interpenetration. And it isn't everything blurring into one. The second lamp is still the second lamp; blow it out, and the first keeps shining. Huayan insists on both halves: each thing is fully itself, in its own place, and each thing holds the whole. Not a soup where everything melts, but a room full of distinct lights, none crowding the others out. On an ordinary day, it's a hard and generous way to look at people: each person whole in their own right, and each one carrying everybody else.

1337.title: The golden lion, deeper
1337.hook: Fazang's teaching: the gold and the lion's shape are one
1337.howItsDone: Students of the Huayan tradition read Fazang's Essay on the Golden Lion as a short introduction to the school's teaching, contemplating the relation of the gold (principle) and the lion (event).

segments.voice: Yesterday, interpenetration: each thing holding all things. Your line: without obstruction. Today, Fazang's lion closes the week.

A wedding ring. A family's old one, maybe, handed down. One day it's too small, so a jeweler melts it and makes it into something new: a pendant. Is the ring gone? The shape is gone; nobody can wear it on a finger anymore. But not one grain of the gold has gone anywhere. It's hanging around somebody's neck. Earlier on this path came Fazang's golden lion, the statue he used to teach an empress, and the basic idea: the gold, the lion's shape, not two. Today, a deeper look. The golden lion.
screen: `A RING, MELTED.` → `THE SHAPE IS GONE. THE GOLD ISN'T.` → `BACK TO FAZANG'S LION.`

segments.voice: In Fazang's essay, the lion doesn't make itself. It appears because a skilled worker shapes the gold. The lion depends on conditions, gold, a hand, a moment, so it has no lion-ness of its own. That's emptiness, the same thing the Tiantai fist showed earlier this week. The gold doesn't change. When the lion is made, the gold gains nothing; when the lion is melted down, the gold loses nothing. Fazang uses that to point at the deep nature of things, which isn't added to when a thing arises or taken away when it ends. Then, looking two ways. When you look at the lion, the essay says, there's only lion; the gold doesn't show. When you look at the gold, there's only gold; the lion doesn't show. See both at once, and both are fully there, hidden and shown together. That is principle and event without obstruction, yesterday's teaching, made into a statue. And every part. The lion's eye is gold, and so is its ear, and so is every hair. Because each part is gold through and through, Fazang says each part holds the whole lion. One hair, the whole beast. Now look back across the week: Tiantai's three truths, Zhiyi's stopping and seeing, Huayan's garland, its lamps that don't crowd each other out, and this lion. Two Chinese schools, two summits, and the same patient work: looking at an ordinary thing until the whole teaching shows through it.
screen: `THE CRAFTSMAN SHAPES THE GOLD.` · `MELTED OR MADE, THE GOLD IS THE SAME.` · `SEE THE LION, OR SEE THE GOLD.` · `EACH HAIR HOLDS THE WHOLE LION.` · then, large: `GOLD AND LION.`

Follow the material back, the wood a branch, and before that a tree drinking rain, then forward, to the day it cracks or burns and becomes something else. Then come back to the thing in your hand, here, now, wood shaped as a spoon.
